Why listed refurbishment is a separate discipline

Listed Building Consent is a legal consent separate from planning permission, governed by the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990. Carrying out works to a listed building without consent, or in breach of a granted consent, is a criminal offence &mdash; not a planning enforcement matter to be regularised after the fact. Even internal works that would be permitted development on a modern property require LBC on a listed one.

The technical discipline is also different. Historic fabric was built to breathe: lime mortars, timber laths and horsehair plaster all move moisture through the wall. Wrapping a Victorian solid-wall in cement render and non-breathable insulation traps moisture, decays timber and causes efflorescence. Sympathetic upgrade uses lime plaster, hemp or sheep's-wool insulation, breathable membranes and secondary glazing that respects the original window.

How we deliver, in order

  1. Pre-application with conservation officerEarly engagement with the borough conservation officer to identify what will and will not be acceptable before design fees are committed.
  2. Heritage statementSignificance assessment, statement of impact and design and access statement prepared for the LBC and any parallel planning submission.
  3. LBC and any planning applicationFormal Listed Building Consent submission, with parallel planning permission where the works involve alteration to the external envelope or a change of use.
  4. Contractor selectionSelection of subcontractors with genuine listed and heritage experience: lime plasterers, traditional joiners, leadwork and slating specialists, conservation-accredited electricians.
  5. Careful strip-out and recordingStrip-out with photographic and drawn recording of anything to be removed; salvage of reusable elements; protection of retained fabric before adjacent works start.
  6. Sympathetic repair and upgradeLike-for-like repair with matched materials, breathable build-ups, secondary glazing, sensitive services routing.
  7. Services & fit-outModern heating, MEP and lighting routed to minimise fabric intervention, with concealed containment through existing voids and chases where possible.
  8. Sign-off & handoverConservation officer sign-off, Building Control completion, warranty pack and O&M covering both modern services and heritage repair techniques.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between Listed Building Consent and planning permission?

Listed Building Consent authorises alteration or extension to a listed building itself, governed by the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990. Planning permission authorises development under the Town and Country Planning Act 1990. Many listed refurbishments need both; some (internal-only) need only LBC. LBC covers internal works that permitted development would allow on an unlisted building.

What do Grade I, II* and II mean?

Grade I buildings are of exceptional interest (about 2.5% of listed buildings). Grade II* are particularly important (about 5.8%). Grade II are of special interest and warrant every effort to preserve them (about 91.7%). Higher grades attract closer scrutiny from the conservation officer and Historic England, and typically require a more restrained approach to intervention.

Can modern additions be permitted on a listed building?

Yes, where the addition is subordinate to the listed building, does not harm its significance, and is clearly of its own time (avoiding pastiche). Contemporary extensions and rooflight additions are routinely consented; the argument turns on the specific significance of the building and the proposed intervention, evidenced through the heritage statement.

What VAT relief applies to listed building work?

The 5% reduced rate of VAT applies to qualifying renovation and alteration works on empty residential properties (usually empty for at least two years). A separate zero-rated VAT relief for approved alterations to listed buildings was withdrawn in 2012, so the standard 20% VAT rate now generally applies to alterations, though 5% may still apply where the property is a qualifying empty dwelling.

Why do you specify lime plaster and breathable materials?

Historic solid walls are designed to move moisture through the fabric. Adding a modern non-breathable finish (cement render, gypsum plaster, PVA-based paint, non-permeable insulation) traps that moisture inside the wall, damages timber, causes rising damp and creates a health hazard. Lime plaster, hemp or wood-fibre insulation and mineral silicate paints preserve the vapour-open build-up the original wall was designed to work in.

What insurance is required for a listed refurbishment?

The contractor's Public Liability and Contractor's All Risks insurance must be sized for the listed property's reinstatement value and specifically extended for works to a listed building, which most standard policies exclude. Existing structures insurance held by the owner is also usually noted for the contract period.
